t: Programming Next Steps: Functions, Lists and AI
l: Hello and welcome to Mr Butler's Digital Technology podcast. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. This is the Year 10 episode for Programming Next Steps: functions, lists and AI.
If you've done the Programming topic, you can already write C sharp console programs with variables, input, if statements and loops.
Today we take the next step. Data types, methods, parameters and return values, scope, arrays and lists, some classic list algorithms, using AI to help with code, and a mini project to finish.
Let's start with a quick recap of data types. A data type tells the computer what kind of value a variable holds.
int is for whole numbers, like the number of goals in a match. double is for numbers with a decimal point, like a height of one point seven two metres.
float also holds decimals, but with less precision, and in C sharp the value needs a letter f on the end. Twelve point five f.
string is for text, in double quotes. char is a single character, in single quotes. And bool, short for Boolean, can only be true or false.
And here's a nice link. Every condition you write, like mark greater than or equal to fifty, works out to true or false. So you can store it in a bool.
Two traps to remember. First, an int divided by an int gives an int. Seven divided by two is three, not three point five.
To keep the decimal, cast one side to a double first. Second trap: phone numbers and postcodes. You never do maths with them, so store them as strings.
Quick, pause and test yourself. What data type would you use to store whether a pupil has paid for the school trip?
A bool. It's only ever yes or no, true or false.
Right, on to methods. Imagine a quiz night program that shows the same three-line banner before every round.
You could copy and paste those three lines eight times. But if the quiz gets renamed, you have to change all eight, and if you miss one, that's a bug.
So instead we write a method. A method is a named block of code that does one job. Other languages call them functions or procedures.
You write it once, and call it whenever you need it. That's the DRY rule. Don't Repeat Yourself.
The header looks like this: static void ShowBanner, open and close brackets. static means it belongs to the program, so Main can call it.
void means it doesn't send any value back. And the name uses PascalCase, with a capital letter at the start of every word.
To call it, you just write ShowBanner, brackets, semicolon. The program jumps to the method, runs it, then comes back to the next line.
The classic mistake is writing a lovely method and never calling it. Nothing happens!
And methods go inside class Program, but outside the curly brackets of Main.
Methods also help with decomposition, which means breaking a big problem into smaller parts. A tuck shop program might be ShowMenu, TakeOrder and PrintReceipt.
Then Main is just three calls, and anyone can see what the program does at a glance.
Next, parameters. What if every round has a different title? We add a parameter: a variable in the method's brackets that receives a value.
So ShowRound, with string title in the brackets. Then we call ShowRound with Round one, Sport, and the next time with Round two, Music.
The value you pass in when you call it is the argument. Here's the memory trick. Parameter, placeholder. Argument, actual value.
You can have several parameters, separated by commas. Like PrintReceipt, with an item, a quantity and a price.
But the arguments must match in three ways: the number of them, the order, and the data type. Put the number two where the item name should go, and it won't compile.
Pause and test yourself. In the call Greet, Sam, fourteen, are Sam and fourteen parameters or arguments?
Arguments. They're the actual values in the call. The parameters are the variables in the method's header.
Now, return values. Some methods do a job. Others work something out and hand the answer back.
Instead of void, you write the type of answer. So static int Square, with int number in the brackets, and inside, return number times number.
Then int answer equals Square of seven stores forty-nine. The call gets replaced by the value it returns.
You can return a double, like an average, or a bool. A method called IsPass could return mark greater than or equal to fifty. Then you can use it right inside an if statement.
Just make sure the value matches the return type. Try to return a double from an int method and you get an error.
And at GCSE you'll hear two words. A function returns a value. A procedure doesn't. In C sharp, they're both just methods.
Next up, scope. The scope of a variable is the part of the program where it can be used.
Think of a whiteboard in one classroom, compared with a notice on the main corridor. Only room twelve sees the whiteboard. Everybody sees the corridor.
A local variable is declared inside a method, or inside a loop. It only exists there. Parameters are local too.
If Main tries to use a variable that was declared inside another method, you get the error: the name does not exist in the current context.
The fix is usually to return the value and store it in Main.
C sharp doesn't really have global variables, but the nearest thing is a static variable declared inside the class, outside every method. Every method can use it.
Handy, but risky. Any method can change it, so a bug in one place can break something somewhere else. Use local variables, parameters and return values where you can.
Right, data structures. Storing twenty-eight test marks in twenty-eight separate variables would be painful.
So we use an array. An array stores a fixed number of values, all the same data type, under one name. Each value is an element, and each element has an index.
And here's the big one. Indexes start at zero. So in an array of five towns, the first is at index zero and the last is at index four.
The last index is always the length minus one. towns dot Length gives you five, but there's no towns of five.
To visit every element, use a for loop. Start i at zero, and keep going while i is less than the length.
If you write less than or equal to instead, the loop tries one element too many and the program crashes with an index out of range exception.
That's called an off-by-one error. And starting at one is the opposite mistake. It quietly skips the first element.
Pause and test yourself. An array has a length of eight. What's the index of the last element?
Seven. Length minus one.
Now, lists. An array has a fixed size, but what about pupils signing up for a trip to the Marble Arch Caves? You don't know how many there'll be.
A list can grow and shrink. You need the line using System dot Collections dot Generic at the top, then something like List of string, names, equals new List of string.
names dot Add puts an item on the end. Remove takes one out. Contains tells you true or false. And Count tells you how many items there are.
Watch out. Arrays use Length, lists use Count. Mixing them up is a really common mistake.
To go through a list, a foreach loop is lovely. For each string player in team. Each time round, player holds the next item.
So when do you choose which? Seven days of the week or twelve months: a fixed number, so an array. A shopping basket or a canteen queue: it changes, so a list.
Next, the classic list algorithms. First, a running total. Start total at zero, then add each item as you go through the list.
The average is the total divided by the count. But remember the trap. Cast the total to a double first, or four hundred and seventeen divided by six gives sixty-nine instead of sixty-nine point five.
To find the largest, start with the first item, not zero, and swap whenever you find something bigger.
Why not zero? Because if all your numbers are negative, like winter temperatures in Fermanagh, nothing beats zero and you'd get the wrong answer.
To count matches, start a counter at zero and add one each time an item meets the condition, like a mark of fifty or more.
And a linear search checks each item in turn, from the start, until it finds the target or runs out of items. A bool called found records whether it turned up.
One more thing: searches are case-sensitive. Erin with a small e won't match Erin with a capital E.
And to check any of these by hand, use a trace table, writing down the value of each variable at every step.
Now the big one for the future: generative AI. Tools like chatbots, or assistants built into Visual Studio, can now write code in seconds.
They learn patterns from huge amounts of existing code and predict what's likely to fit your request. But they don't run your program to check it works.
The benefits are real. Speed, explaining error messages in plain English, suggesting ideas. Like a patient tutor.
But AI can be confidently wrong. It can make off-by-one errors, use integer division in averages, forget a using line, or even invent methods that don't exist.
That last one is called a hallucination.

In the notes there's an AI average method that looks perfectly tidy. But it uses less than or equal to in the loop, so it crashes. And even after fixing that, integer division gives fourteen instead of fourteen point seven five.
So how do you get better results? Write a good prompt. Say the language, the exact task, the inputs and outputs, your level, and ask it to explain each line.
Then verify. Read every line, and if you can't explain it, don't use it. Trace it. Test it. Check it does exactly what the task asked. Then refine.
And be honest. Handing in AI-written code as your own work is plagiarism. For GCSE coursework, the work must be your own and any AI use has to be acknowledged.
Also, never paste personal data into an AI tool, like real pupils' names and marks. What you type might be stored by the company.
Best tip? Use AI as a tutor, not a ghost-writer. Ask it why an error happens, or for a hint, not the whole answer.
Finally, the mini project: a class quiz-score analyser. Mr Butler types in scores out of twenty, and gets the count, the average, the highest score and how many passed.
It's built in a software development cycle. Plan, develop, test, refine, and go round again.
The plan uses decomposition. GetScores returns a list. CalculateAverage returns a double. FindHighest and CountPasses return ints.
Then you build in small stages and test each one, so if something breaks, you know it was the bit you just added.
The test table uses three kinds of test data. Normal data, like thirteen. Boundary data, at the very edge, like zero and twenty. And erroneous data, like twenty-five or the word ten.
Pause and test yourself. Scores must be from zero to twenty. Is twenty-one normal, boundary or erroneous?
Erroneous. It's outside the allowed range, so the program should reject it.
Before refining, three tests failed. Twenty-five was accepted, typing the word ten crashed it, and entering no scores at all crashed it too.
So we refine. Add validation to reject scores outside zero to twenty. Use int dot TryParse, which returns false instead of crashing when the text isn't a number. And check if the count is zero first.
Then, and this is important, run the whole test table again, because a fix can sometimes break something else.
Let's recap. A data type decides what a variable can store, and an int divided by an int gives an int.
Methods avoid repetition. Parameters pass values in, and return sends one value back.
Local variables only exist inside their own method or block, so prefer them to globals.
Arrays have a fixed size and start at index zero. Lists can grow and shrink, and use Count.
AI can help, but always read, trace and test its code, and be honest about using it.
And build programs in stages, with a test table of normal, boundary and erroneous data.
That's Programming Next Steps. Now go and try the quizzes on each page, and have a go at the code yourself in Visual Studio.
Happy coding, and thanks for listening. See you next time.
